clue.text: Sticks together in the vote

explanation.surface: Some voters hang together as a bloc when the ballot comes.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'faggot vote' was a nineteenth-century electoral trick: property was split up so that extra men qualified to vote, and such a voter was called a faggot.
explanation.definitionFit: A bundle of firewood bound together is the old meaning; the second is the historical term for a voter given a sham property qualification.

clue.text: Pale and no longer fiery like a bird

parts.note: as means like, in the sense 'just as'
a hen is a female bird, typically the farmyard chicken

explanation.surface: A bird described as having lost its fire and gone pale.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition has two halves: grey-white in colour, and burnt out like a fire that has gone to ash.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey-white like the residue of a burnt-out fire describes a face drained of colour.

clue.text: Even God takes in information in this university

parts.note: Gott is the German word for God, fitting a German university town
taken as written
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A claim that even the deity goes to college to be informed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' and 'takes' are link words; the German word for God is the clue's hint that the university is German. Göttingen is a famous university town in Lower Saxony.
explanation.definitionFit: Göttingen in Germany is home to one of Europe's best-known universities, founded in 1734.

clue.text: Distributing tithes, when she wasn't immersing her son ?

indicators.note: distributing spreads the letters of the fodder around into a new order

explanation.surface: Church dues being handed out by a mother when not busy bathing her boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distributing' rearranges TITHES. The sea-nymph Thetis dipped her son Achilles in the river Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the sea-nymph who dipped baby Achilles in the Styx was his mother.

clue.text: Small county of high degree for deer-stalkers ?

parts.note: Bucks is the short form of Buckinghamshire, an English county north-west of London
hot means at a high degree of temperature

explanation.surface: A minor county with an exalted rank, asked about in a hunting context.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of high degree' suggests social rank, but it means a high temperature. The definition is cryptic: coarse shot is literally ammunition for bucks, male deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Coarse lead pellets were traditionally used for shooting deer, hence the name.

clue.text: Froth at the mouth, then split — coming out of the frying-pan ?

parts.note: to bubble is to froth, as at the mouth
and means then, as in 'and next'
to split or squeak is old slang for informing on someone to the police

explanation.surface: Someone raging until they finally turn informer, and escaping a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: BUBBLE AND SQUEAK is a British dish of leftover cabbage and potato fried together; the name is said to come from the noises it makes in the pan.
explanation.definitionFit: The British leftover dish of mashed potato and cabbage is fried, so it comes out of a pan.

clue.text: There's many a neat, rustic lover at the helm

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so many
neat is an old word for cattle, so a neat is an ox
a swain is a country youth or suitor in pastoral poetry

explanation.surface: A tidy country lad steering a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Neat' looks like an adjective meaning tidy, but it is the archaic noun for cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: The steersman of a rowing boat or ship's boat is the one who steers it.

clue.text: Office workers use this bar for the interval

explanation.surface: Typists reaching for a key to mark a gap.
explanation.walkthrough: On a typewriter the long bar at the bottom of the keyboard puts a gap between words.
explanation.definitionFit: The typewriter's spacebar makes a blank; an interval is a gap of distance or time.

clue.text: Uncomfortably fill the position of a demagogue

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser packing out a hall beyond comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the word in two: a demagogue stands above the masses he harangues.
explanation.definitionFit: To pack a place with too many people; and standing above the masses is where a rabble-rouser sits.

clue.text: Many a tea-time host has to take his fists to him, he's so talkative

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so many
the Mad Hatter hosts the tea party in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
to box someone is to hit them with the fists

explanation.surface: A man so talkative that the host of a tea party wants to punch him.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition stands for a person who talks a great deal: he is so talkative he is one.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who never stops gossiping or prattling is called this.

clue.text: The war-god's measures

explanation.surface: Asking what the god of war's units of measurement are.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is' joining the two definitions. An are is a metric unit of area, 100 square metres.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek god of war; and the plural of a metric unit of land area equal to a hundred square metres.

clue.text: Anti-pop ?

parts.note: pop is a father, so being against your father is behaving badly as a son or daughter, not pop music

explanation.surface: Someone against pop music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' is not music here but the familiar word for dad.
explanation.definitionFit: Failing in the duty a child owes a parent is the opposite of dutiful conduct toward father.

clue.text: An honourable man pursues Jenny with a blunt instrument

indicators.note: pursues puts the honourable man after Jenny, following her

parts.note: Jenny is the traditional pet name for the female wren, Jenny Wren
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A distinguished man chasing a woman called Jenny while armed with a cosh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jenny' looks like a woman's name, but Jenny Wren is the folk name for the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanner is a heavy tool that could serve as a blunt weapon.

clue.text: Shooting-irons are turned on the beast

indicators.note: are turned tells you the guns' slang name is read backwards

parts.note: gats is gangster slang for guns, from Gatling

explanation.surface: Hunters aiming their guns at an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are turned on' paints guns aimed at the animal, but 'are turned' reverses GATS.
explanation.definitionFit: A male deer is the beast in question, the classic quarry of shooting.

clue.text: Comb it out, if tangled in Africa

indicators.note: if tangled says the letters of the fodder are knotted into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to comb out hair should it get knotted, somewhere in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If tangled' rearranges COMB IT OUT. Timbuctoo, now usually Timbuktu, is a city in Mali.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabled desert city in Mali is a place in Africa, an old byword for remoteness.

clue.text: Magnificent male sport

parts.note: recalls the film Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines, whose heroes' pastime was flying

explanation.surface: A grand masculine game.
explanation.walkthrough: The 1965 film Those Magnificent Men in their Flying Machines is about early aviators competing in a London-to-Paris air race.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying aircraft was the pastime of the magnificent men of the film title.

clue.text: Ability to endure a permissible error

explanation.surface: Patience described as an acceptable mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: In engineering the second sense is the allowed margin by which a measurement may vary.
explanation.definitionFit: Endurance of pain or hardship; and in engineering, the allowed margin of variation in a measurement.

clue.text: And the rest is classical

parts.note: the phrase meaning 'and so on' is Latin, a classical language

explanation.surface: A remark that everything remaining belongs to the classical canon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classical' does not mean music here; it means the phrase is Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'and other things', said when a list goes on.

clue.text: What's come out from the man at Edinburgh ?

indicators.note: from tells you the letters are taken out of the words of the man at Edinburgh

explanation.surface: Asking what has emerged from a Scottish gentleman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' lifts the run out of thE MAN AT EDinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that has issued or flowed out from a source has come out.

clue.text: Diarist in trouble with her twins

annotationWithheld.why: Diarist in trouble with her twins (4): LEDA is the mother of the twins Castor and Pollux, but no reading of 'Diarist' gives LEDA or its letters, and no anagram fodder in the clue has four letters.
annotationWithheld.clue: Diarist in trouble with her twins

clue.text: This dog has his days

parts.note: the dog days of high summer were named for the star of the Dog constellation rising with the sun

explanation.surface: A twist on the saying every dog has his day.
explanation.walkthrough: The dog days of July and August are named after the Dog Star, which rises with the sun at that season.
explanation.definitionFit: The brightest star in the night sky lies in Canis Major and is called the Dog Star.

clue.text: Confusion of a stubborn type without twopence

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the stubborn beast is wrapped around the coins

parts.note: a mule is proverbially stubborn
d was the old British abbreviation for a penny, so two pence is two Ds

explanation.surface: A muddle-headed obstinate person who is broke, lacking two pennies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking' but means outside. Pre-1971 British pennies were written d, from Latin denarius.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess or disorder is a state of confusion.

clue.text: Do we need money for a pin ?

parts.note: L stands for pound, the British currency unit, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Asking whether cash is needed to buy a pin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Need' joins the pieces. L is the pound sign, from libra.
explanation.definitionFit: A wooden peg used to join two pieces of timber is a kind of pin.

clue.text: Leave with a tear — it's due to the Lord of the Manor

definitions.text: it's due to the Lord of the Manor

parts.note: to quit is to leave
a rent is a tear or rip in cloth

explanation.surface: Someone departing in tears, while a feudal lord collects what is owed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' reads as a teardrop but is a rip. A quitrent was a small fixed rent paid to the lord of a manor in place of feudal services.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fixed payment freed a tenant from feudal service to the manorial lord.

clue.text: A home-bird, she ?

parts.note: a bird that stays home keeps to its nest; the girl's name sought is what such a stay-at-home would be called

explanation.surface: A woman who likes to stay at home.
explanation.walkthrough: A stay-at-home bird is a nester, and the girl's name Nesta is said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A Welsh girl's name, here suggested by one who keeps to her nest.

clue.text: Pack for the point-to point

parts.note: S is south, one point of the compass
taken as written
W is west, another point of the compass

explanation.surface: Packing for a cross-country horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: A point-to-point is a British amateur steeplechase, but here each 'point' is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To put things away neatly for travel is to pack them.

clue.text: The fly at the inquest on a flier

definitions.text: The fly at the inquest on a flier

parts.words: The fly at the inquest on a flier
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme Who Killed Cock Robin, the fly says it saw the bird die with its little eye

explanation.surface: An insect present at an inquiry into an airman's death.
explanation.walkthrough: The flier is Cock Robin; in the rhyme 'Who saw him die? I, said the Fly, with my little eye, I saw him die.'
explanation.definitionFit: One who sees an event and can testify about it, as the fly in the rhyme did.

clue.text: Support for the lordly president

parts.note: the person presiding over the House of Lords sits on a large wool-stuffed cushion

explanation.surface: A grand chairman's backing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lord Chancellor, who presided over the British House of Lords, sat on a large wool-stuffed seat, a symbol of England's medieval wool trade.
explanation.definitionFit: The wool-filled cushion seat of the presiding officer of the House of Lords supports him.

clue.text: Observe the cutter go up and down

parts.note: to see is to observe
a saw is a cutting tool

explanation.surface: Watching a blade rise and fall.
explanation.definitionFit: To move alternately up and down like a playground plank is to rock.
